View in browser             Sponsored by       Lingling Wei   As Trump and Xi Meet, Spin Is on the Agenda   Plus, the U.S. invites Putin to G-20 at a Trump resort in Florida, and conservative podcasters lose interest in Trump     KENT NISHIMURA/AFP/GETTY IMAGES   Good morning. I’m The Wall Street Journal’s chief China correspondent, filling in for Damian Paletta.

   President Trump and China’s Xi Jinping are meeting in Washington for their second summit of the year, and expectations are low. Both sides have played down the odds of “deliverables” —diplo-speak for concrete outcomes—signaling they care more about a smooth meeting than the deep differences between the world’s two largest economies.

   Then, just on Wednesday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent hinted at something bigger. “The Chinese on Sunday came up with the idea of a bigger deal,” he said following a New York meeting with Vice Premier He Lifeng, Xi’s economic right-hand man. “We’re open to the idea of just continuing the Busan arrangement or examining the bigger deal.” He meant the one-year trade truce the two leaders struck last October in Busan, South Korea, which halted a tariff war and expires in November.

   But being “open to the idea” isn’t a promise. Read another way, Bessent’s remark is less a sign that a grand bargain is near than an indication of the U.S. leverage over China. Chinese officials have incentives to dangle the prospect of more so the meeting doesn’t end up looking like it failed to deliver much.

   Still, something might come out of it. People close to the Chinese side told me Beijing has weighed bigger purchases of American farm goods to please Trump before November’s midterms, and held back until now so Xi could head home with a win.

   What does China want in return? Beijing rarely gives anything away for free. Xi will keep pressing Trump to oppose Taiwanese independence and halt arms sales to the self-ruled democracy. And there is the lever Beijing cares about most: U.S. export controls. Could either be in play?

   For more, including takeaways from today’s summit, sign up for my WSJ China newsletter .

   This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here . 

       People and Policies I’m Watching   White House media ban: A federal judge ordered Trump to temporarily restore access to the building for CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists.

   Mark Carney: The Canadian prime minister said that a Canada-U.S. trade pact was still possible, but that his country won’t give up its freedom to strike deals with the EU and other parts of the world.

   Energy costs: Energy Secretary Chris Wright and GOP Reps. Dan Meuser and Ryan Mackenzie are set to discuss U.S. energy production in Allentown, Pa.

   Trump’s Thursday: The president is hosting Xi for a state visit, with both leaders scheduled to deliver remarks at 10:15 a.m. ET, and then to hold bilateral meetings at 11:30 a.m. and noon. At 7:55 p.m., Trump and Xi will again deliver remarks, and have a state dinner at 8:10 p.m.

The administration has been making an effort to bring Russia back into Group of 20 leaders meetings , with the Russian president last having attended a G-20 summit in 2019 in Japan. Some congressional Republicans pushed back on the idea of welcoming Putin to the U.S., with Sen. John Cornyn (R., Texas) calling the Russian leader a “killer.”

   Conservative podcasters seem to be losing interest in Trump. Instead, they are criticizing Senate candidate James Talarico, the Bible-quoting Democrat threatening to flip red Texas, and they can’t stop debating the Lindsay Clancy murder trial. The Journal analyzed nearly 70,000 hours of podcasts to understand the topics that conservative podcasters are talking about as the midterm elections approach.

Dan Osborn, who is running as an independent for the U.S. Senate, has tried to cast himself as an outsider who can take on both parties. But in audio recordings that were leaked , Osborn can be heard describing Trump supporters in unflattering terms and suggesting he can’t honestly state his views for fear of alienating GOP voters.

       What Else Is Happening   • Eight Navy personnel assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide during its deployment in the fight against Iran.

   • The tech industry is calling on the Trump administration to withdraw a new H-1B visa fee .

   • Benjamin Netanyahu’s visit to the United Nations poses a challenge for New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

   • The energy secretary said the administration wouldn’t ban exports of diesel but rather implement voluntary caps.

   • The Trump administration is planning to smooth the way for more tobacco products such as flavored vapes to legally enter the market .

White House media ban: A federal judge ordered Trump to temporarily restore access to the building for CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists.

What I’m Following

The U.S. invited Vladimir Putin to a Trump resort in Florida in December for the G-20 meeting. The administration has been making an effort to bring Russia back into Group of 20 leaders meetings, with the Russian president last having attended a G-20 summit in 2019 in Japan. Some congressional Republicans pushed back on the idea of welcoming Putin to the U.S., with Sen. John Cornyn (R., Texas) calling the Russian leader a “killer.”

 

Conservative podcasters seem to be losing interest in Trump. Instead, they are criticizing Senate candidate James Talarico, the Bible-quoting Democrat threatening to flip red Texas, and they can’t stop debating the Lindsay Clancy murder trial. The Journal analyzed nearly 70,000 hours of podcasts to understand the topics that conservative podcasters are talking about as the midterm elections approach.

Dan Osborn, who is running as an independent for the U.S. Senate, has tried to cast himself as an outsider who can take on both parties. But in audio recordings that were leaked, Osborn can be heard describing Trump supporters in unflattering terms and suggesting he can’t honestly state his views for fear of alienating GOP voters.
